theme: Sing to the LORD a new song, David’s psalm at the ark
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 96. You read this in Unit 3 as a song of the nations. Notice that much of it is quoted in 1 Chronicles 16, where David first gave it to Asaph, and read it now as the missionary song of the returned people.
settingTheScene: Psalm 96 appears almost word for word in 1 Chronicles 16:23-33. The Chronicler included it because it captures the heart of David’s worship: a song that sends praise to the whole earth. A small, fragile community, rebuilding in a corner of the Persian empire, still sang that God is king over all nations. That is the faith of the returned exiles. They did not shrink their God to fit their circumstances.
observation: “Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth!” (v. 1).
“Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day” (v. 2).
“Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!” (v. 3).
“For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods” (v. 4).
“For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens” (v. 5).
“Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength” (v. 7).
“Say among the nations, The LORD reigns!” (v. 10).
“He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm is a missionary hymn. Its first three verses are a chain of commands: sing, bless, tell, declare. The song is not meant to stay in the temple. The goal is to tell the nations. This was an extraordinary thing for a small people to say. They had nothing to boast about: no army, no king, no wall until recently. And yet they said, “Declare his glory among the nations.”

The reason is who God is. He is great and above all gods. The gods of the peoples are “worthless idols,” a word that plays on “elilim,” meaning “nothings.” But the LORD made the heavens. The contrast is between nothing and the Maker. Having heard Psalm 115 only a few days ago, you recognize the theme.

Then the psalm calls the “families of the peoples” to ascribe glory to the LORD and to bring an offering and come into his courts. The nations are not simply an audience; they are invited to worship. This is the vision first given to Abraham: “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

The announcement at the center is the best news: “Say among the nations, The LORD reigns!” The heavens rejoice, the earth is glad, the sea roars, the fields exult, and the trees of the forest sing for joy. All creation celebrates because he is coming to judge. The judgment is good news: it means that wrongs will be set right, the oppressed will be vindicated, and the world will finally be put in order. He will judge “in righteousness” and “in his faithfulness.”

You read this in Unit 3 as an invitation. Today, remember that the people who sang it were few and weak. And God used them.
connection: Genesis 12:3 promises that all families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. Matthew 28:19-20 sends the disciples to make disciples of all nations. Acts 17:30-31 says God will judge the world in righteousness by a man he has appointed. Revelation 7:9-10 shows people from every nation praising God. Romans 10:14-15 asks how people will hear without a preacher. Revelation 11:15: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.”
application:
Tell someone this week one thing about God that you believe is good news for them.

Pray for a missionary or a people group that has not heard.

Sing or read the psalm aloud outdoors, joining the trees of the forest.
prayerPrompts: Sing to the LORD a new song, in your own words.
Tell him he is greater than every other thing you are tempted to rely on.
Ask him to help you declare his glory.
